:::{#thm-spectral}
#### Spectral theorem for symmetric matrices

If $\matr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix (@def-symmetric-matrix)
with real entries,
then there are a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ (@def-orthogonal-matrix)
and a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix $\matr{\Lambda}$ (@def-diagonal-matrix)
with real diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$ such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{p \times p}
= \underbrace{\matr{Q}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\matr{\Lambda}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{Q}}}_{p \times p}
$$

Each $\lambda_i$ is an eigenvalue of $\matr{A}$ (@def-eigenvalue),
and column $i$ of $\matr{Q}$ is an eigenvector of $\matr{A}$ for $\lambda_i$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-spectral-equivalent-form}
#### An equivalent form of the spectral theorem

The proof, by induction on $p$, is outside the scope of these notes;
see @banerjee2014linear [Chapter 11, Theorem 11.27, p. 349],
which states the result in the equivalent form
$\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q} = \matr{\Lambda}$.
The two forms are equivalent because
$\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q} = \matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p$
(@rem-orthogonal-matrix-columns).
Multiplying $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
by $\tp{\matr{Q}}$ on the left and by $\matr{Q}$ on the right gives

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q}
&= \tp{\matr{Q}}\paren{\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}}\matr{Q}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q}}\matr{\Lambda}\paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(regroup; matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p\matr{\Lambda}\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(} \matr{Q} \text{ is orthogonal)}
\\
&= \matr{\Lambda}
&& \text{(identity matrix)}
\ea
$$

and multiplying $\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q} = \matr{\Lambda}$
by $\matr{Q}$ on the left and by $\tp{\matr{Q}}$ on the right
gives back $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$ the same way.

For example, let
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
and
$\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$,
which is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{Q}$.
Then

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q}
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute; multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 + 1 & 1 + 2 \\ 2 - 1 & 1 - 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication, first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 + 3 & 3 - 3 \\ 1 - 1 & 1 + 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add; multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

a diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ of $\matr{A}$
from @exm-eigenvalue on its diagonal.

:::
